5.08 Effects on Wildlife. The resultant minor loss of wildlife habitat associated with initial but isolated downstream bank sloughing should constitute the impact upon the wildlife. This impact is not expected to significantly affect the wildlife resource along the Rio Grande.
5.09 Effects on Fishery. Although hydroelectric releases will increase the volume and duration of daily flows downstream of Amistad Reservoir, abrupt changes in several water quality parameters may cause fish stress for some undetermined distance below the dam. During the hot summer months and early fall, when Amistad Reservoir is stratified, temperature shock, low dissolved oxygen, and possibly hydrogen sulfide will cause most of the impacts on the fishery. As discussed in a previous section (see paragraph 4.38), the exact reach of the Rio Grande that will be seriously affected by hydropower releases during critical periods is not truly known. However, on the basis of visual evidence, weirs in the river at 2.2 and 12.6 miles should add significant oxygen to releases. Additionally, during a test release that approximated modeled hydropower releases, the temperature recovered at about 9 miles below the dam (Parker, et al., 1976). On the basis of these two parameters alone, minor effects on river fisheries should probably be limited to that reach above Del Rio, with the more significant effects possibly occurring in the first 2.2 miles downstream because of negligible oxygen during critical periods.
5.10 Effects on Historical and Archeolgical Resources. Since there are no known existing or proposed historic landmarks, sites, or markers having National, State, or regional significance within the project's area of influence, there should be no adverse impacts upon these resources.
5.11 Socioeconomic Effects. There will be a theoretical but insignificant loss of water through evaporation as a result of changing the mode of operation at Amistad and Falcon Reservoirs.
